text:
Zohran Mamdani, New York City’s mayor, announced on Monday that the city has reached an agreement with Lyft, the parent company of Citi Bike, the city’s bike-share system, to cap ebike fares for members at $3.65 for rides of up to 45 minutes, starting in mid-January.
In a video announcing the changes, the mayor’s office said that a 45-minute ebike ride currently costs members $12.15, but that under the new agreement, that price will fall to $3.65 from 19 January 2027.
“This cap will significantly reduce the cost of roughly 5 million rides taken by New Yorkers annually,” Mamdani said at a news conference on Monday. “If this cap had been in place just last year alone, it would have saved New Yorkers $10,932,958.”
As part of the deal with Lyft, Lyft will also freeze the annual Citi Bike membership fee, which stands at $239 a year, through May 2029, when the company’s current contract with the city expires.
“Today’s announcement is a critical step towards making biking affordable for every New Yorker,” Mamdani said. “And it’s a part of our city hall’s larger goal to make life more affordable in every way we can for those who call our city home.”
Patrick Knoth, general manager of Citi Bike, welcomed the changes in a statement on Monday: “Every day, New Yorkers choose Citi Bike to get to work, to school, and to each other, and this cap gives even more of them the chance to get around their city by bike.”
As part of the deal, the city has agreed to work with Lyft to help upgrade and install on-site electric charging infrastructure at Citi Bike stations, beginning at 130 stations next year. This will allow the ebikes to recharge while docked, rather than requiring workers to drive around the city swapping out batteries.
The city will also allow Lyft to run advertising across “all bike station display panels starting on 1 January of next year,” Mamdani said on Monday. He also said “when it comes to revenue share”, the company “will only start to pay the city whatever exceeds $5.25bn a year” and “no longer have to reimburse us for lost parking meter revenue”.
There were on average of about 169,000 Citi bike rides a day in September, according to data shared by Lyft and the city’s department of transportation (DOT). According to that data, about 139,400 people have annual Citi Bike memberships.
Over the years, the cost of Citi Bike trips has risen significantly. Members currently pay $0.27 per minute for ebike rides, meaning that a 45-minute journey costs $12.15. In 2021, by comparison, the same ride cost members $4.50, according to the New York Times. There are some exceptions, such as that ebike rides of up to 45 minutes for members that enter or exit Manhattan are capped at $5.40. This new agreement will replace that.
Additionally, the new agreement helps the city move closer to fare parity across all major forms of transit as now subways, buses, ferries and ebikes all roughly cost about the same per ride.
The changes announced on Monday will not extend to non-members, whose prices will remain the same. A 45 minute ebike ride for someone without a membership can cost more than $18, in addition to a $4.99 unlock fee, according to the New York Times.
Asked at Monday’s press conference whether the city had plans to make Citi Bike more affordable for non-members, Mamdani said that “today, around 82% of City Bike users are members and one of the things that we’ve heard from New Yorkers who have not yet signed up to be members is they’re concerned that the cost of membership continues to increase year after year.
“And so, one of the reasons that we focused on going beyond the 365 was to freeze membership costs,” he said, adding that “the price that they’re looking at today is the price that it will be in the years to come, and that that could actually deliver them some sense of stability”.
Mamdani also noted that recipients of the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (Snap) as well as residents of New York City Housing Authority (Nycha) public housing, are eligible for Citi bike memberships costing just $5 a month.
